\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{むこう} (mukou)}{むこう (mukou)}]{\ja{むこう} (mukou) — the other side}

\label{lesson:JA-C79-mukou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for beside, then the Japanese for the very middle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{むこう}}
\textbf{\ja{むこう}} — \emph{mukou} — \textquotedblleft{}the other side\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{むこう}} (\emph{mukō}) is native, from \emph{mukau}, \textquotedblleft{}to face, to head towards\textquotedblright{} (JMdict writes both with the same character). It is inherited rather than borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Japanese for beside, then the Japanese for the very middle, then say \emph{mukou} again
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{てまえ}}
\textbf{\ja{てまえ}} — \emph{temae} — \textquotedblleft{}this side of\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\ja{てまえ}} (\emph{temae}) is a native compound, inherited rather than borrowed: \emph{te}, \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{mae}, \textquotedblleft{}front\textquotedblright{}: what is in front of your hand (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{かど} (kado)}{かど (kado)}]{\ja{かど} (kado) — a corner}

\label{lesson:JA-C79-kado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for the other side, then the Japanese for this side of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{かど}}
\textbf{\ja{かど}} — \emph{kado} — \textquotedblleft{}a corner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{かど}} (\emph{kado}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{かいだん} (kaidan)}{かいだん (kaidan)}]{\ja{かいだん} (kaidan) — stairs}

\label{lesson:JA-C79-kaidan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for this side of, then the Japanese for a corner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{かいだん}}
\textbf{\ja{かいだん}} — \emph{kaidan} — \textquotedblleft{}stairs\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{かいだん}} (\emph{kaidan}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{kai}, \textquotedblleft{}stairs, storey\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{keaj}) and \emph{dan}, \textquotedblleft{}step, section\textquotedblright{} (\emph{dwanH}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart).
\end{cousinweb}
